title: ParetoProof: When Does Pareto Selection Improve Lean Proof Maintenance?
content: When a proof system finds several correct proofs, which one should it keep? A short proof may be fragile, while a robust proof may be slower or depend on more of the library. Pareto selection is meant for such tradeoffs, but it can only help when the available proofs actually disagree on the objectives. We study this question in Lean using 649 natural maintenance units with 1,649 valid candidates. Only 160 units (24.7%) have more than one nondominated candidate, and 75 (11.6%) show high objective conflict. Among 312 units with later-version results, ParetoProof improves survival over equal-weight scalarization by 3.5 percentage points (78.5% versus 75.0%, p=0.0207), but its 1.3-point advantage over adaptive scalarization is not statistically detectable (p=0.424). A post-hoc analysis suggests that Pareto selection becomes more useful as objective conflict grows, although this pattern requires prospective confirmation. A separate LLM-assisted generation study over 16 theorem families explains why the average benefit is small: even after 32 generations, each theorem has 9.5 distinct verified proofs but only 3.31 nondominated choices on average. Our practical conclusion is simple. When the likely maintenance failure is known, optimize the matching proxy. When objectives mostly agree, adaptive scalarization captures nearly all observed benefit. Conflict-rich pools are the setting in which Pareto selection should be tested prospectively.
